kabul: Kabul lies at an altitude of 1,791 m in a narrow valley of the Hindu Kush, along the Kabul River, in the eastern part of Afghanistan. South of the old city stand the ancient city walls and the Sher Darwaza mountain, and further east the ancient fortress of Bala Hissar. The city lies on the trade routes of Central Asia and South Asia and is traditionally seen as the meeting point between Tartary, Hindustan and Persia.

The origin of Kabul, who built it and when, is largely unknown, though it is believed to be over 3,500 years old. The Rigveda and the Avesta refer to the Kabul River and to a settlement called Kubha. Greek writers called it Kophen or Kophes. After Cyrus the Great annexed the Median Empire in 549 BCE, Kabul became part of the Achaemenid Empire and a centre of learning for Zoroastrianism, followed by Buddhism and Hinduism. An inscription on the tomb of Darius the Great lists it among the 29 countries of that empire.

After Alexander the Great annexed the Achaemenid Empire, the valley passed to the Seleucid Empire, which in 305 BCE ceded Gandhara, including the Kabul Valley, to the Maurya Empire. Trade flourished under Mauryan uniform weights and measures. Later empires that claimed Kabul include the Kushan, Ghaznavid, Ghorid and Timurid. In the 16th century the Mughal rulers used it as their summer capital, and it prospered.

Kabul became part of the Durrani Empire in 1747 and the capital of Afghanistan in 1776 under Timur Shah Durrani. British forces occupied it briefly in the First and Second Anglo-Afghan Wars. In the second half of the 20th century it was a stop on the hippie trail and was nicknamed the Paris of Central Asia. The Saur Revolution of 1978 and the Soviet intervention of 1979, which began a ten-year war, ended that period, and a civil war among mujahideen factions in the 1990s destroyed much of the city. The Taliban captured it in 1996.

Kabul is the capital and largest city of Afghanistan and has long been its political, cultural and economic centre. Its people speak mainly Dari and Pashto. Historical gardens and palaces include the Arg, Bagh-e Babur, Bagh-e Bala, Chihil Sutun, Darul Aman and Tajbeg.
kakusthavarma: Kakusthavarma, also written Kakusthavarman, was a son of King Bhageerath, the third ruler of the Kadamba dynasty. When his father died the throne passed to his elder brother Raghu, and Kakusthavarma became Yuvaraja, or crown prince. As heir apparent he held a court of his own, perhaps at Palashika, the present-day Halasi, from where he is known to have issued land grants. In due course he succeeded his brother as king.

His reign is noted above all for its marriage alliances. The marriage of one daughter, read as a marriage into the imperial Gupta family, is counted the most important. It is also likely that another daughter married the Vakataka prince Narendrasena: Vakataka records describe Narendrasena's wife, Ajjhitabhattarika, as a princess of the Kuntala country, which probably corresponds to the Kadamba kingdom. Through such ties the Kadambas stood in close diplomatic relations with the great royal houses of India. The Talagunda and Halmidi inscriptions praise the king as a formidable warrior.

He appears also to have been a builder and a patron of both secular architecture and religious causes. He is described as owning numerous palaces adorned with gopuras. The Talagunda pillar inscription of his son Santivarma records that he had a great water tank made near a Shiva temple at which Satakarni and other kings of the past had worshipped. His own leanings seem to have been Jain: his grant at Halasi opens with an invocation to Jinendra, the lord of the Jinas, and he probably patronised a Jain temple there.

On his death the kingdom appears to have been divided among his descendants. One son, Santivarma, succeeded him at Banavasi and ruled the northern part of the realm. Another, Krishnavarma I, seems to have founded a junior branch of the dynasty at Triparvatha, in the south. The height of Kadamba power under Kakusthavarma was therefore followed by a kingdom held in two lines.
kansas: Kansas is a landlocked state on the Great Plains, bordered by Nebraska to the north, Colorado to the west, Oklahoma to the south and Missouri to the east. It is generally considered the geographic centre of the contiguous United States, with Lebanon in Smith County approximately the centre. Its highest point is Mount Sunflower, at 1,231 m. The name comes from the Kansas River, named after the Kansa or Kaw people, and ultimately from the Algonquian term Akansa, which referred to the Quapaw.

Before European colonisation the area was occupied by the Caddoan Wichita and later the Siouan Kaw. In the east, people generally lived in villages along the river valleys, while those in the west were semi-nomadic and hunted large herds of bison. The first European to enter present-day Kansas was the Spanish conquistador Francisco Vázquez de Coronado, who explored the area in 1541. Between 1763 and 1803 the territory was part of Spanish Louisiana. Most of modern Kansas was acquired by the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, and the south-west was ceded after the Mexican–American War in 1848.

From 1812 to 1821 Kansas was part of the Missouri Territory. The Santa Fe Trail crossed it from 1821 to 1880, carrying manufactured goods from Missouri and silver and furs from Santa Fe, and wagon ruts from the trail are still visible in the prairie. The first settlement of non-Indigenous people took place in 1827 at Fort Leavenworth, and settlement quickened in the 1850s during the political wars over slavery.

The Kansas–Nebraska Act officially opened Kansas to settlement in 1854. Conflict then broke out between abolitionist Free-Staters from New England and pro-slavery settlers from neighbouring Missouri over whether it would be a free or a slave state, a period known as Bleeding Kansas. Kansas entered the Union as a free state on 29 January 1861, whence the unofficial nickname The Free State. The Homestead Acts of 1862 brought further settlers, and the cattle trade of the 1870s drew some of the best-known figures of the Wild West to the west of the state. From 1887 Kansas women could vote in city elections and hold certain offices.

Topeka is the capital and Wichita the most populous city, while the largest urban area is the Kansas City metropolitan area, which straddles the border with Missouri. The 2020 census counted 2,937,880 people. Nearly 90 per cent of the land is devoted to agriculture, with wheat, corn, sorghum and soybeans among the main crops, and the state also has a large aerospace industry. Kansas is the setting of Dorothy Gale's home in The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900), and its state anthem is Home on the Range, written by Brewster Higley.
karachi: Karachi lies on the coastline of Sindh province in southern Pakistan, along the Karachi Harbour, a natural harbour on the Arabian Sea. It is built on a coastal plain with scattered rocky outcroppings, hills and marshlands, and mangrove forests grow in the brackish waters around the harbour and farther south-east towards the Indus River Delta. West of the city is Cape Monze, known locally as Ras Muari, an area of sea cliffs, sandstone promontories and beaches. Two small ranges, the Khasa Hills and the Mulri Hills, lie within the city in the north-west. They are barren, part of the larger Kirthar Range, and reach a maximum height of 528 metres.

The region has been inhabited for millennia. Upper Paleolithic and Mesolithic sites have been excavated in the Mulri Hills on the northern outskirts, and their earliest inhabitants are believed to have been hunter-gatherers who left ancient flint tools. The region is believed to have been known to the ancient Greeks and may have been the site of Barbarikon, an ancient seaport at the nearby mouth of the Indus. Karachi may also be the place called Ramya in ancient Greek texts.

The modern city was reputedly founded in 1729 as the fortified village of Kolachi-jo-Goth during the rule of the Kalhora dynasty, said to be named in honour of Mai Kolachi, whose son slew a man-eating crocodile. The shortened name Karachee was first used in a Dutch report of 1742 about a shipwreck near the settlement. The village greatly increased in importance with the arrival of the East India Company in the mid-19th century, following the annexation of Sindh. The colonial administration began substantial projects to turn it into a major seaport and to connect it to the railway network of South Asia.

At independence in 1947 Karachi was the largest city in Sindh, with an estimated 400,000 people and a slim Hindu majority. After the partition of British India, hundreds of thousands of Muslim refugees arrived from India while nearly all its Hindu residents left. Karachi served as the federal capital of Pakistan from 1947 to 1959 and grew rapidly, attracting migrants from across the country and other parts of South Asia.

Karachi is the capital of Sindh and the largest city in Pakistan, with about 20 million people according to the census of 2023. It contains the country's two largest seaports, the Port of Karachi and Port Qasim, and its busiest airport, Jinnah International Airport. It is one of the most linguistically, ethnically and religiously diverse cities in Pakistan. Among its landmarks are Frere Hall, Empress Market and St. Patrick's Cathedral, which brought the first neo-Gothic buildings to the city, and Wazir Mansion, the birthplace of Muhammad Ali Jinnah, now a museum.
karl-marx: Karl Marx was born on 5 May 1818 to Heinrich Marx and Henriette Pressburg at Brückengasse 664 in Trier, then part of the Kingdom of Prussia. His family was originally Jewish but had converted to Christianity before his birth. His father, a lawyer, had converted to the state Evangelical Church of Prussia to keep his career after Prussia annexed the Rhineland and Jewish emancipation was abrogated. Heinrich was a man of the Enlightenment and a classical liberal who took part in agitation for a constitution and reforms.

Marx was the third of nine children and became the eldest son when his brother Moritz died in 1819. He was baptised into the Lutheran Church on 28 August 1824. His father educated him privately until 1830, when he entered the Gymnasium zu Trier. Its headmaster, Hugo Wyttenbach, employed many liberal humanists, and in 1832 police raided the school and found literature promoting political liberalism among the students. Marx earned a doctoral degree in philosophy from the University of Jena in 1841, then turned to radical journalism.

In Paris Marx wrote his Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and began a close collaboration with Friedrich Engels. After moving to Brussels they were active in the Communist League. In London Marx wrote the Grundrisse notebooks and the three volumes of Das Kapital, the second and third of which Engels published after his death, in 1885 and 1894. He became a leading figure in the International Workingmen's Association, and in 1875 wrote the Critique of the Gotha Programme.

His thought drew on Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel's dialectic, on the classical political economy of Adam Smith and David Ricardo, and on French socialist thought. Unlike Hegel, who saw spirit driving history, Marx argued for the primacy of matter over idea. He held that societies develop through class conflict, in capitalism between the bourgeoisie who control the means of production and the proletariat who sell their labour power for wages, and he criticised utopian socialists for relying on small-scale communities.

Marx died on 14 March 1883 and was buried in Highgate Cemetery. His ideas had a profound impact on world politics after the Russian Revolution of 1917. His followers have often disagreed over how to interpret him, and tendencies including Leninism, Marxism–Leninism, Trotskyism, Maoism and Luxemburgism each claim to be his most accurate interpreter. In scholarship his work contributed to the birth of modern sociology, and Isaiah Berlin considered him the true founder of the discipline in so far as anyone can claim the title.
kathiawar: The peninsula covers about 61,000 square kilometres and faces the Arabian Sea on the south and south-west. From the heads of its two gulfs the Little Rann of Kutch and the waste tracts of Khambhat, half salt morass and half sandy desert, reach inland towards each other, so that only one narrow neck on the north-east joins Kathiawar to the mainland of Gujarat. Two belts of hill country cross it, and nine rivers drain it radially; they carry little water outside the monsoon months, and dams have been built on some of them. Most of the natural vegetation is dry scrub. The region has also been called Sorath.

The name Kathiawad seems to derive from the early settlements of the Kathis, who entered Gujarat from Sindh in the early centuries of the Common Era; Saurashtra comes from Sanskrit words meaning good nation. In the reign of Chandragupta Maurya the region was governed by Pushyagupta, and under Ashoka by the Yavana Tushaspa. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, of the first century CE, calls the coast Syrastrene and describes a fertile country yielding wheat, rice, sesame oil, clarified butter and cotton cloth, with many cattle. The Junagadh rock inscription attributed to Rudradaman I, dated to 150 CE, also mentions the region.

After Indian independence in 1947, 217 princely states of Kathiawar, among them the former Junagadh State, were merged on 15 February 1948 into the United State of Kathiawar, renamed Saurashtra State in November 1948. Vallabhbhai Patel spent much time persuading the princes; Maharaja Krishnakumar Sinhji of Bhavnagar State was the first to offer his state. Rajkot was the capital and Uchharangray Navalshankar Dhebar the first chief minister. On 1 November 1956 Saurashtra was merged into Bombay state, and when that state was divided along linguistic lines in 1960 it became part of Gujarat.

The region now comprises eleven districts of Gujarat, with part of Ahmedabad district; historically it also took in Diu. Gir National Park and its surroundings hold the last remaining population of Asiatic lions, and the peninsula has two further national parks, the Blackbuck National Park at Velavadar and the Marine National Park in the Gulf of Kutch. Severe droughts have repeatedly left farmers without crops or drinking water. A campaign to build check dams from the late 1990s raised water tables, but in 2019 a severe drought struck again and water had to be brought by tanker from the Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada River.
kathmandu: Kathmandu lies in the northwestern part of the Kathmandu Valley, north of the Bagmati River, at an elevation of about 1,324 metres. The city covers 50.7 square kilometres and is bounded by Lalitpur, also called Patan, with which it forms one urban area surrounded by a ring road. It is dissected by eight rivers, of which the main one is the Bagmati. The valley is an ancient lake basin with fertile soil and flat terrain, which helped form a society based on agriculture.

Its position between India and China made it an important trading centre. Trade flourished along an offshoot of the Silk Road linking India and Tibet, and Lhasa Newar merchants of Kathmandu conducted trade across the Himalaya and helped spread art styles and Buddhism across Central Asia.

Archaeological excavations in Kathmandu have found evidence of ancient civilisations. The oldest finding is a statue from Maligaon dated to 185 CE. The excavation of Dhando Chaitya uncovered a brick with an inscription in Brahmi script, which archaeologists believe is two thousand years old. Historically the valley was known as the Nepal Mandala and was the cultural and political hub of the Newar people. From ancient times until the medieval period Kathmandu was known as Kantipur, which derives from Sanskrit words meaning beauty and place, giving the sense of city of light.

The name Kathmandu comes from Kasthamandap, a public pavilion made of wood, from the Sanskrit words for wood and pavilion. It was rebuilt in 1596 in the period of King Lakshmi Narasimha Malla, and according to legend all its timber came from a single tree. The earliest Western reference to the city is in the account of the Portuguese Jesuit Father Joao Cabral, who passed through the valley in the spring of 1628 and was received by the king, probably Lakshminarasimha Malla. He reported that they reached Cadmendu, the capital of the kingdom of Nepal.

Kathmandu is the capital and largest city of Nepal and its main governmental, financial, industrial and cultural centre. The 2021 census recorded a population of 845,767, with approximately 4 million in the surrounding metropolitan area. Its people are multi-ethnic, with a Hindu majority and a significant Vajrayana Buddhist presence. Since 1985 it has hosted the headquarters of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation.

Hindu and Buddhist practice has influenced the monuments of the city over the centuries. In 2006 UNESCO declared seven groups of monuments in the valley a World Heritage Site, among them Durbar Square, Swayambhu Mahachaitya, Bouddha and Pashupatinath.
kigeli-iv-rwabugiri: Rwabugiri, whose birth name is given as Sezisoni Rwabugiri, was a Tutsi of the Nyiginya dynasty, which traced its line back to Gihanga, one of the first kings whose deeds are celebrated in Rwanda's oral chronicles. His year of birth is uncertain and is given as about 1840. He held authority from 1867 to 1895 and was among the last kings of his line.

Around 1870 Rwabugiri established a royal court at Rubengera that collected labour dues and tribute in food. It channelled food across the country and became a centre of commerce. The court managed production so as to keep a surplus as a provision against famine, and on the king's order this was distributed to the poorest in exchange for their labour; in times of shortage, however, the very rich Tutsi living at Rubengera could find food and livestock while most of the country suffered.

As he annexed new lands he placed appointed chiefs over them, drawn into a network that bound the regions to the court. These chiefs sometimes met local resistance: in the north-west the Balera challenged the Nduga whom the court had installed, a contest along lines of clan, since both groups were then counted as Tutsi. Several annexed districts, such as Bugoyi, Bwishaza and Kingogo, had been inhabited entirely by Hutu, and Tutsi moved into them in numbers afterwards. He also killed chiefs of his own Nyiginya lineage who had shown too much independence.

He was the first king of Rwanda to come into contact with Europeans. He built an army equipped with guns obtained from Germans and barred most foreigners, especially Arabs, from the kingdom, defending its borders against neighbouring kingdoms and slave traders. By the end of his rule the country was divided into provinces, districts, hills and neighbourhoods under a hierarchy of chiefs.

Rwanda had been assigned to the German Empire at a conference in Brussels in 1890, but no expedition came until that of Count Gustav Adolf von Götzen in 1894. Rwabugiri died in September 1895 on an expedition in what is now Congo. His son Rutarindwa was proclaimed king as Mibambwe IV, with Kanjogera of the Bega clan, another of Rwabugiri's wives, as queen mother. With her brother Kabare she carried out a coup at Rucunshu in which Rutarindwa was killed, and made her own son king as Yuhi V Musinga. The weakened state opened the way to direct German colonisation in 1897.
kinshasa: Kinshasa stands on the southern shore of Pool Malebo, a widening of the Congo River, in a broad crescent of flat, low-lying terrain at an average elevation of about 300 metres. The city-province covers 9,965 square kilometres, and the Congo River forms its western and northern boundary with the Republic of the Congo. Across the river, about four kilometres away and unbridged, lies Brazzaville, so that the two capitals are the closest pair in the world. The river is a transport route across much of the Congo Basin, with barges navigable between Kinshasa and Kisangani.

The site has been inhabited by Teke and Humbu people for centuries. In pre-colonial times it held two trading centres, Ntamo and Ntsaasa, which were part of the Tio Kingdom. Two theories explain the name Nshasa. One links it to a bag of salt, and to a trading post where people from the lower Congo and the Atlantic exchanged salt for goods including ivory and enslaved people; the other derives it from Teke trading terms, in which fishermen exchanged fish for cassava.

The city was founded on 1 August 1881 as Léopold II Station, and Henry Morton Stanley named it Léopoldville in honour of Leopold II of Belgium. A royal decree of 11 April 1914 designated it the capital of the Belgian Congo, and an ordinance of 25 June 1941 gave it city status. Its population grew from 5,000 in 1889 to 39,530 in 1930 and reached 400,000 at independence in 1960.

In 1966, during Mobutu Sese Seko's Zairianisation campaign, it was renamed Kinshasa as a tribute to the village of Nshasa. Its economic prominence peaked in the 1970s, a period known as la belle époque, and in 1974 it hosted the boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman known as the Rumble in the Jungle.

Kinshasa is the capital and largest city of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with a population estimated at about 18 million. It is also one of the country's 26 provinces, divided into 24 communes. French is the language of government, education and the media, while Lingala is the lingua franca of the street. UNESCO designated it a City of Music in 2015, and it has a long-established music scene and a national stadium, the Stade des Martyrs.
kiribati: Kiribati has a total land area of 811 km2 spread over 3,441,810 km2 of ocean. Its islands, from Banaba in the west to Kiritimati in the east, straddle the equator and the 180th meridian. They fall into three groups: the Gilbert Islands, sixteen atolls about 1,500 km north of Fiji; the Phoenix Islands, eight atolls and coral islands; and the Line Islands, eight atolls and one reef. Banaba is a raised coral island that was once a rich source of phosphates. The rest of the land is sand and reef rock islets that rise only one or two metres above sea level, with thin, calcareous soil. Kiritimati has the largest land area of any atoll in the world.

The area has been inhabited by Austronesian peoples speaking the same Oceanic language since sometime between 3000 BCE and 1300 CE. Oral historians suggest that seafarers from Melanesia came first, later visited by Austronesian seafarers from the west. Around 1300 CE a mass departure from Samoa added Polynesian ancestry and culture. From about the 15th century the northern islands came under chiefly rule (uea), while the central and southern islands were ruled by councils of elders (unimwaane); Tabiteuea alone is known to have kept an egalitarian society. Clans and chiefs fought over land, and some islands used guns and cannon-equipped ships supplied by Europeans to destroy their foes.

The name Gilbert Islands was given around 1820 by the Russian admiral Adam von Krusenstern and the French captain Louis Duperrey, after the British captain Thomas Gilbert, who sighted some of the islands in 1788. The British annexed the Gilberts as a protectorate in 1892. From 1916 the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony took its name from them, and it lasted until the Ellice Islands became Tuvalu in 1976. Kiribati became independent from the United Kingdom in 1979, with the Gilberts, the Phoenix and Line islands and Banaba. The name is the Gilbertese rendering of Gilberts. Phosphate mining on Banaba was exhausted by independence, and the Banabans mostly live on Rabi in Fiji.

Kiribati is a parliamentary democratic republic under the constitution promulgated on 12 July 1979. Its capital, Tarawa, is made up of islets joined by causeways, and more than half the population lives there. A census of November 2020 counted 119,940 people. The I-Kiribati are a Micronesian people who speak Gilbertese, an Oceanic language; English is the other official language. The country joined the United Nations in 1999.
kobayakawa-clan: The Kobayakawa claimed descent from the Taira clan, through its Kanmu-Heishi branch, which traced itself to Emperor Kanmu, the 50th emperor of Japan. Nakamura Munehira, son of Taira no Tsunemune, founded the Nakamura clan of Sagami Province. His second son, Dohi Sanehira, who died in 1191, founded the Dohi clan, and Sanehira's second son, Kobayakawa Tohira, who died in 1237, founded the Kobayakawa. Two sons of the third head of the family, Kobayakawa Shigehira, who died in 1264, divided the clan: Masahira, his third son, made his base at Numata and began the Numata-Kobayakawa, and Masakage, his fourth son, settled at Takehara and began the Takehara-Kobayakawa.

The two branches continued side by side for some three centuries; the lists of their heads end with the same man, Kobayakawa Takakage, born in 1533, the third son of Mōri Motonari. Takakage was the uncle of Mōri Terumoto, and his brother headed the allied Kikkawa clan, so that the Kobayakawa held great power in the politics of western Japan. Toyotomi Hideyoshi regarded Takakage as one of the best statesmen and appointed him to the Council of Five Elders, but Takakage died in 1597, before Hideyoshi.

At the end of the 16th century the Kobayakawa fought beside the Kikkawa, Mōri, Toyotomi and Ōtomo clans against the Shimazu for control of Kyūshū, and after the defeat of the Shimazu they were awarded Chikuzen Province as their fief. Takakage's successor, Kobayakawa Hideaki, born in 1582, was a nephew of Hideyoshi.

A powerful clan of the Sengoku period, the Kobayakawa were disbanded in the Edo period, after the Battle of Sekigahara. In the Meiji period the Mōri clan restored the house, which was given the title of baron in the new nobility. The Kusai clan of Takehara, a branch of the Kobayakawa, was also granted noble rank.
kolkata: Kolkata lies on the eastern bank of the Hooghly River in the lower Ganges Delta, at an elevation of 1.5 to 9 metres. Much of the city was originally a wetland, reclaimed over the decades to accommodate a growing population. Excavations at Chandraketugarh, 35 kilometres to the north, show that the region has been inhabited for over two millennia. The name derives from Kôlikata, the Bengali name of one of three villages that predated the British, the others being Sutanuti and Govindapur. One explanation is that it varies Kalikshetra, the area of the goddess Kali.

The earliest mention of the village of Kalikata is in Bipradas Pipilai's Manasa Vijay of 1495. The three villages were part of an estate belonging to the Sabarna Roy Choudhury family of zamindars, sold to the East India Company in 1698. The city's recorded history began in 1690 with the arrival of the Company. Job Charnock is often regarded as its founder, but in 2003 the Calcutta High Court ruled, in response to a petition, that the city has no founder.

The Company developed the area into Fort William. Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah occupied the fort in 1756 but was defeated at the Battle of Plassey in 1757. Under Company and then crown rule Calcutta was the de facto capital of India until 1911 and, after London, the second largest city of the British Empire. It was the centre of bureaucracy, politics, law, education, science and the arts, was associated with the Bengali Renaissance and was a hotbed of the Indian nationalist movement. The first newspaper in India, the Bengal Gazette, began publishing there in 1780.

The partition of Bengal in 1947 affected the city's fortunes, and Hindu refugees from East Bengal arrived in the following decades. In 1971 it hosted Bangladesh's government-in-exile. Its official name, Calcutta, was changed to Kolkata in 2001.

Kolkata is the capital and largest city of the Indian state of West Bengal, with a city population of about 4.5 million and a metropolitan area of over 15 million. Its landmarks include the Victoria Memorial and the Howrah Bridge. The University of Calcutta was the first modern university in South Asia, and the Port of Kolkata is India's oldest operating port. The city's celebrations of the festival of Durga Puja are recognised by UNESCO.
kosovo: Kosovo covers 10,887 km2 in the centre of Southeast Europe. Most of its borders run along mountains, notably the Accursed Mountains in the west, a continuation of the Dinaric Alps, and the Šar Mountains in the southeast. Between them lie two major plains, the Kosovo Plain in the east and the Metohija Plain in the west. The name comes from Kosovo Polje, Blackbird Field, the karst field where the Battle of Kosovo was fought in 1389. In the Middle Ages the western territory was called Metohija, because large portions of land belonged to Serbian Orthodox monasteries and Mount Athos; Albanians call it Dukagjini.

The earliest evidence of organised settlement belongs to the Neolithic Starčevo and Vinča cultures. In antiquity the area was the core of Dardania, named after the Dardani, a Paleo-Balkan people usually described as Illyrian, though scholars debate whether they were Illyrian or Thracian. Dardania was incorporated into the Roman Empire in the 1st century BCE and became a separate Roman province in the 3rd century CE. Under the Byzantines the region faced Slavic migrations in the 6th and 7th centuries, and control passed between the Byzantines and the First Bulgarian Empire.

In the 13th century Kosovo became integral to the medieval Serbian state and the establishment of the Serbian Patriarchate. Ottoman expansion in the late 14th and 15th centuries brought the fall of the Serbian Empire, and the Battle of Kosovo of 1389, in which a Serbian-led coalition fought the Ottoman Empire, is regarded as one of its defining moments. Various dynasties, chiefly the Branković, governed afterwards. The Ottoman Empire fully conquered Kosovo after the Second Battle of Kosovo and ruled for nearly five centuries until 1912. The Ottoman Vilayet of Kosovo, created in 1877, was the first time the name was applied to a wider area.

Kosovo was a centre of the Albanian Renaissance and saw Albanian revolts in 1910 and 1912. After the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913 it was ceded to the Kingdom of Serbia, and after the Second World War it became an Autonomous Province within Yugoslavia. Tensions between the Albanian and Serb communities culminated in the Kosovo War of 1998 and 1999, after which the Yugoslav Army withdrew and the United Nations Interim Administration Mission in Kosovo was established.

Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia on 17 February 2008. Its recognition is partial, and Serbia does not officially recognise it as a state. The capital and largest city is Pristina, and the euro is the official currency. Four Serbian Orthodox churches and monasteries, including Visoki Dečani, the Patriarchate of Peja, Our Lady of Ljeviš and Gračanica, are inscribed as the World Heritage Site Medieval Monuments in Kosovo.
krasnodar: Krasnodar stands on the right bank of the Kuban River, about 1,300 km south of Moscow, with the Black Sea 120 km to the west. The climate is humid subtropical. Winters are cold and damp with unstable snow cover, the July average is 24.1 °C, and about 735 millimetres of rain and snow fall in a year. No mountains shield the city from cold waves, so winter temperatures below −20 °C are not uncommon.

The city began in 1793 as a military camp and then a fortress built by the Black Sea Cossacks to defend the imperial borders and to assert Russian dominion over Circassia, a claim that Ottoman Turkey contested. Its name, Yekaterinodar, meant Catherine's Gift, recognising both Catherine the Great's grant of land in the Kuban to the Cossacks and Saint Catherine of Alexandria, regarded as the city's patron. It received town status in 1867 and by 1888 had about 45,000 people. The 1897 census counted 65,606, of whom 52.9 per cent spoke Russian and 38.3 per cent Ukrainian.

During the Russian Civil War the city changed hands several times between the Red Army and the Volunteer Army. The White general Lavr Kornilov besieged it on 10 April 1918 and was killed a week later when a Bolshevik shell destroyed the farmhouse that served as his headquarters. On 7 December 1920 it was renamed Krasnodar, meaning Gift of the Reds. The city lost over 14 per cent of its population in the Soviet famine of 1932–1933.

German forces occupied Krasnodar from 9 August 1942 to 12 February 1943. The city was heavily damaged, and the Gestapo and mobile SS execution squads killed thousands of Jews, Communists and suspected partisans. From 14 to 17 July 1943 a Soviet tribunal at Krasnodar tried people for collaboration and war crimes and pronounced eight death sentences, carried out in the city square before a crowd of about thirty thousand.

Krasnodar is the largest city and administrative centre of Krasnodar Krai, with a population of 1,154,885 within the city limits. The 2021 census counted one million people there for the first time. The historic centre keeps buildings from the 19th century, and the city has St Catherine's Cathedral and a steel lattice hyperboloid tower built by the engineer Vladimir Shukhov in 1928. It is the home of the Kuban Cossack Choir and of the Kovalenko Krasnodar Regional Art Museum, the oldest public art museum in the North Caucasus.
kuala-lumpur: Kuala Lumpur lies in the Klang Valley, bordered by the Titiwangsa Mountains in the east and the Strait of Malacca in the west. It stands at the confluence of the Klang and Gombak rivers, in the centre of Selangor on the central west coast of Peninsular Malaysia. The municipality covers 243 square kilometres, and its highest point is Bukit Nanas at 94 metres.

The name means muddy confluence in Malay, from kuala, the point where two rivers join, and lumpur, mud. Its origin is uncertain. One suggestion is that it was named after a Sungai Lumpur, a muddy river. Others propose Pengkalan Lumpur, muddy landing place, or a Cantonese word, lam-pa, for flooded jungle, but there is no firm contemporary evidence for these.

Kuala Lumpur was first developed around 1857 by Raja Abdullah as a town serving the tin mines of the region. Yap Ah Loy and Frank Swettenham were instrumental in its early development in the late 19th century. In 1872 Swettenham described the settlement beside the Klang River as a purely Chinese village, though a Malay stockade already stood at Bukit Nanas. It was the capital of Selangor from 1880 until 1978. Most of its notable colonial-era buildings date from the end of the 19th century and the early 20th, among them the railway station and the Jamek Mosque.

The city belonged to the Federated Malay States from the late 19th century, was under the Empire of Japan from 1942 to 1945, and became part of the Malayan Union in 1946 and the Federation of Malaya in 1948. It was the founding capital of the Federation of Malaya and of Malaysia, formed in 1963. It received city status in 1972, and in 1974 it was separated from Selangor to become the first Federal Territory. Its federal executive and judicial branches moved to Putrajaya in early 1999.

Kuala Lumpur is the capital and most populous city of Malaysia, with 2,111,536 people. It is the seat of the Parliament of Malaysia and of the Istana Negara, the official residence of the monarch. Its population includes the Malays, Chinese and Indians as well as Eurasians, Kadazans, Ibans and other Indigenous peoples. The Petronas Towers are the tallest twin buildings in the world, and the University of Malaya, established in 1949, is the oldest university in Malaysia.
kuntillet-ajrud: Kuntillet Ajrud, also known by the Hebrew name Horvat Teman, was one of the few water sources along the Darb el-Ghazza, the Gaza Road, which ran from the site of ancient Eilat or Ezion-Geber past Kuntillet Ajrud and Kadesh Barnea up to Gaza. Carbon-14 dating indicates that the site was occupied from 801 to 770 BCE.

The main building is fortress-like and divided into two rooms, one large and one small, both with low benches. Both rooms held paintings and inscriptions on the walls and on two large water jars, or pithoi, one found in each room.

What the site was for is disputed. It is frequently described as a shrine, though this is not certain. The excavator, Ze'ev Meshel, first argued for a religious function from the inscriptions and drawings with religious themes and from an unusual amount of linen, which he connected with the dress of priests. Other scholars point out that the site has no temple, shrine or cultic objects, and that similar textiles have since been found at Kadesh Barnea. Four inscriptions carry the military title Commander of the Fortress, three on storage jars and one on the plastered walls, which supports the view that it was a state-sponsored fortress or a caravanserai.

Although its position in the Sinai would normally point to the Kingdom of Judah, the occupants are usually taken to have come from the northern Kingdom of Israel. The evidence is the pottery, the personal names with the ending -yaw, the northern spelling of some inscriptions and the references to Yahweh of Samaria.

Edward Henry Palmer identified the place in 1869, when it was known as Contellet Garaiyeh, with the station Gypsaria on the Tabula Peutingeriana, and noted the remains of an ancient fort. Ze'ev Meshel of Tel Aviv University excavated it in 1975 and 1976, and the excavation report was published in 2012.

The paintings on the pithoi show animals, stylised trees and human figures. They appear to have been made over a considerable period by several artists and form no coherent scenes. Talley Ornan has argued that all the drawings have parallels in Neo-Assyrian palace reliefs and were preliminary sketches for wall paintings, and Schniedewind has read the inscriptions as scribal exercises of soldiers stationed at the fortress. Mordechai Gilula's theory that two figures on one jar represent Yahweh and the goddess Asherah has been almost abandoned: the scholars who have analysed the images in most detail hold that they are Bes or Bes-like figures.
kyiv: Kyiv lies on both banks of the Dnieper River, which flows southward through the city toward the Black Sea. The older and higher western part sits on wooded hills with ravines and small rivers, and these gave the city toponyms such as Podil (lower), Pechersk (caves) and uzviz (a steep street). The city expanded onto the low left bank to the east only in the 20th century. Its name is traditionally derived from Kyi, one of four founders named in tradition, though the linguist Jaroslav Rudnyckyj reads it as meaning palisaded settlement.

The first people in the region lived there in the late Paleolithic. Roman coins of the 2nd to 4th centuries suggest trade with the eastern provinces of the Roman Empire. Scholars debate when the city was founded. The traditional date is 482 CE, so the city marked its 1,500th anniversary in 1982, while archaeology points to the sixth or seventh century, and some researchers date it as late as the late 9th century. In the Primary Chronicle the brothers Kyi, Shchek and Khoryv and their sister Lybid are the founders.

A Slavic settlement on the trade route between Scandinavia and Constantinople, it was a tributary of the Khazars until its capture by the Varangians in the mid-9th century. Under Varangian rule it became a capital of Kievan Rus', the first East Slavic state. The Siege of Kiev in 1240 left it in ruins, and it lost most of its influence for centuries. It grew into a centre of Eastern Orthodox learning in the 16th century, and the Mohyla Academy was founded as a theological school in 1632.

The city prospered during the Industrial Revolution of the Russian Empire in the late 19th century. In 1918 the Ukrainian People's Republic declared independence and made Kyiv its capital. After the Ukrainian-Soviet and Polish-Soviet wars it became part of the Ukrainian SSR, whose capital it became in 1934. It suffered significant destruction in World War II and recovered as the third-largest city of the Soviet Union. It became the capital of independent Ukraine in 1991.

Kyiv is the capital and most populous city of Ukraine, with 2,952,301 inhabitants in January 2022. It has a special legal status as a city that is also treated as a region of the country. It remains a centre of Eastern Orthodox Christianity, and the Saint Sophia Cathedral and the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, the Monastery of the Caves, form a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Taras Shevchenko University, founded in 1834, is the oldest university in continuous operation there.
